comment: Same matter, overlapping time: the Commission (October 2024) says EU supplementary pension rules for mobile workers are not in Moldovan law; the Government (December 2025) says the law is aligned with Directive 2014/50/EU. The Government text cites no new law since the 2024 report (it points to Law 198/2020, which predates it) and itself says Moldova has no occupational pension scheme. The Government claim rests on CNPF conformity tables (a self-assessment), but as stated the two cannot both be true.

Different instruments: the Commission says EU citizens no longer need a work permit since January 2024; the Government says they still need a temporary residence permit for work purposes. The same 2024 report counts residence permits for work granted to EU citizens, and the 2026 report refers to the old temporary stay-for-work regime, so the two claims concern different documents, not the same requirement. The basis (stays up to 90 days) is not supported by either text.

Different dates and formal stages: in 2024 the agency was named coordination body for preparatory EURES work; in September 2025 it was formally designated National Coordination Office. This is a sequence rather than a conflict; same_as_earlier or no link would also be defensible.

Different measures: 10,290 is all residence permits (the IGM report also gives 3,525 extensions on top of 7,043 new temporary residence decisions), while 7,043 counts new temporary residence decisions only. The IGM figure of 11 is a purpose category ("foreigner from an EU member state"), not a count by nationality, so it does not measure the same thing as 783 EU citizens.

Different measures: IGM ranks countries by all temporary residence purposes, where family reunification puts Russia and Ukraine near the top. The Commission list (Nepal, Türkiye, Uzbekistan first) matches the IGM work-purpose figures (Nepal 710, Uzbekistan 682, Türkiye 623). Bangladesh does not appear in the IGM top five, so the Commission figure may also come from another series.

Different surveys and measures: IOM (cited by ETF) gives 49% employed in January to March 2024; UNHCR gives 29% in paid work from the SERHC 2024 survey. The definitions (employed against paid work) and samples differ. Not a link between independent claims about the same quantity.

Different (unstated) reference dates for the same indicator: 447 against 445 of 636, a difference of two services. Neither source dates its count, and the Commission report covers to September 2026 while the news item is from August 2026.

Different reference dates: the 166 single sign-on figure is the 2023 Strategy figure repeated in the Reform Agenda; the May 2025 draft programme gives a current count of 303. The Reform Agenda figure is stale, not contradictory. Single sign-on and direct access may also differ in definition.

Different reference dates and definitions: the Commission figure covers to June 2023 ("online public administrative services") and SIGMA (October 2023) counts e-services through servicii.gov.md out of 718 registered services. The counts are close and not dated.

Different measures and dates: 166 is e-services with single sign-on in the Strategy (baseline data from about 2022), while 276 is all e-services available through the portal per SIGMA in 2023. Single sign-on is a subset.

Different measures: the Commission figure is "services mapped" (an unstated denominator) and is undated; the Ministry gives more than 50% of public services by end 2023 (52.8% in its own table). The Commission figure equals the Strategy 2022 baseline of 40%, so it is probably an older baseline. Worth noting at G6 as stale Commission data, but not proven to be the same measure at the same date.

Closest to a confirmed conflict in this set: the indicators are very similar (essential business services online; essential online services for companies). But the Reform Agenda 30% is undated and sits next to World Bank data, while the Ministry gives no 2022 value and 55.2% for 2023. A different source and an earlier reference period is the likely explanation; the analyst may prefer confirmed.

Probably different survey editions: SIGMA gives the 2022 UN EGDI rank 72; the Strategy calls its benchmark 79 "2022", and its context page lists other rankings, so it probably carries the 2020 survey rank. The Strategy text does not say this, so the analyst should check.

Same document, same matter: IPRE says the Strategy sets 75% of public services digitised by end 2024, but the Strategy table sets 80% by 2026 and 100% by 2030. The Strategy text has no 75%-by-2024 target for public services; 75% appears only for essential business services and for systems in MCloud, both by 2026. IPRE misreports the target, possibly from a draft.

Different documents and dates: the May 2025 draft programme states a 75% by end 2026 aim, while the 2023 Strategy table says 80% by 2026. This is most likely a restated or revised target in the later programme, although the programme presents it "as part of the Strategy". Not a factual conflict about the situation.

Not a stated conflict: 118 minus 18 gives 100, against 104 in 2024, only by the checker's arithmetic. Closures or counting only "active" centres (the 2026 report says "118 CUPS active") would explain it. Neither source states an end-2024 figure that conflicts.
Different definitions of launch: 2017 and 2018 are commonly the pilot and the full (mandatory) launch of MTender. Neither text says which. Minor, and both are outside the evidence window.

Probably adoption date against publication date: Government Decision 650/2023 was adopted on 6 September 2023 (White Book) and published in Monitorul Oficial no. 383-386 in mid-September; IPRE gives 14 September. Check the decision on legis.md if the date matters.

Different versions of the cost estimate: 654 million lei comes from the May 2025 draft programme, and 613 million lei from the December 2025 draft update of the National Accession Programme (whose own annex gives 615 million). The uncovered 225 million lei is the same in both. A revision between drafts is the likely explanation.

Same matter, overlapping period: SIGMA (October 2023) says all state information resources and systems have been registered; the Court of Accounts audit (September 2024, covering 2021 to mid-2024) finds registration of all systems delayed and its recommendation only partly implemented. The audit is the more authoritative and later source, but the claims conflict.

Different measures and dates: SIGMA's 4/4 scores the existence of formal coordination arrangements in 2023; the 2025 programme judges the effectiveness of coordination. A formal arrangement and ineffective coordination can both be true.

Different reference dates and counts: IPRE cites an MDED platform for entrepreneurs (523 services, 226 digitalised, undated 2023); the Strategy gives 517 G2B with 204 online on 31 March 2023. The two figures are close and probably from different dates of the same series. The G2C figures are a separate population.

Same author (MDED), same measure (service requests in 2023, online and at the counter), different figures: 3.7 million with 2.48 million online in the May 2024 report, against 4,524,731 with 3,058,794 online in the May 2025 draft. A data revision is likely but is not stated. The 2025 figures also do not add up (noted at extraction).
Different measures: 30% of "essential" business services (undated, Reform Agenda) against 64% of all public services for businesses in 2024 (Commission). Essential services are a subset.
Different measures: 30% of essential business services (undated) against 65.7% of all G2B services digitalised in early 2025.

No conflict: the Commission says a new integrated information system was being developed in December 2025, with fully digital services aimed for 2027 (in_progress). ANOFM says it currently lacks a modern system. Both can be true.

Same event, one day apart (23 against 24 August 2026), most likely a day-counting convention for entry into force (a period counted from publication). Trivial; not worth a contradicts link unless the date matters.

No conflict: the Commission says Moldova "continued to align" with NIS 2, including through new secondary legislation, and makes no claim of non-alignment. The Government says NIS 2 was transposed by Law 48/2023 and GD 562/2025. The government wording is stronger, but the Commission text does not contradict it.

Two different decision numbers for the establishment of the Cybersecurity Coordinating Council (GD 1186/2023 in the July 2024 factsheet, flagged possible_misread; GD 333/2024 in the National Accession Programme). They may be successive acts (one replacing the other) or a numbering error. Not resolvable from the texts; check on legis.md.

Different measures and dates: 30 employees recruited (MDED report on 2025) against 32 staff employed by December 2025 (Commission, March 2026). Staff not recruited in that action, such as management, may explain the difference.
Different dates: 8 employed in the CERT directorate during 2025 (MDED) against nine specialists "currently" active (Commission, March 2026).
Different measures: 38 incidents handled (Commission) against 40 incidents recorded in the notification register (agency). Recorded incidents need not all be handled ones.

Different measures of alignment: the Government says Law 72/2025 transposed the EECC, and Promo-LEX says the final law states only partial compatibility. The government sentence does not say fully transposed, so it is an overstatement more than a contradiction. Borderline; the analyst may prefer confirmed.

Different reference points: Freedom House assesses the 2007 law (amended 2017) against older EU directives ("largely harmonised"); the Commission speaks of alignment with the 2018 EECC and the roaming acquis, which "has started". Both can be true.

Different measures: the Commission (report to September 2025) says "not aligned" with the geo-blocking and P2B acquis; the Government (December 2025) says Law 54/2025 partially transposes the Geo-blocking Regulation. A partial transposition, possibly not yet assessed or in force, is compatible with a finding of non-alignment. Borderline; check the law's dates of adoption and entry into force.

Same law, two numbers: the National Accession Programme gives Law 54/2025 as the geo-blocking law and consistently names Law 53/2025 the platform-to-business (online intermediation) law (four places). The MDED 2025 progress report calls Law 53/2025 the geo-blocking law. One is a numbering error, probably in the progress report.

Different data sources and methods for the same year: ITU (63.5% of individuals using the internet in 2022) against the Strategy (more than three in four citizens in 2022, source not stated). The Commission's "39% do not use" is consistent with ITU.

Different reference years and sources: 80% using the internet in 2021 (Strategy, national source) against about 39% not using it (Commission 2023, consistent with ITU 2022). This is a measurement difference, but the gap is large; the analyst should note that national and international internet-use figures diverge.

Different measures: 98% of localities have fibre-optic links (backbone reaching the locality, 2023 Strategy) against fibre-optic networks available in about 75% of localities (access networks, undated 2025). The Strategy itself says high-speed home access is still a challenge.

Different measures: 88.1% of households connected according to a 2023 survey of individuals aged 18 and over (AGE) against 74.1% of households with internet access (undated, probably official household statistics). The MDED 2025 programme gives 825.2 thousand of 1.1 million households (about 75%), which supports the 74.1% figure.
Different definitions and dates: 431 localities are "white areas" without fixed broadband per provider data (2025), against about 370 villages unable to connect to optical internet (2024).

Different calculation formulas, documented in the source: ANRCETI's recalculation (accepted by MDED in the 2025 programme) gives 37.8% for 2023 against 51.8% in the 2024 report. A method revision, not a conflict of fact; the 2024 figure is superseded.

Different measures: 57% high-speed broadband coverage (population covered, Commission) against 45.1% of the population with 100 Mbps connectivity (subscriptions, ANRCETI formula). Coverage and take-up differ.

No conflict of substance: ARCOM writes "Consiliul Europei" (Council of Europe) where the Council of the EU is meant, as the extraction note already says. Both sources agree that Moldova joined Roam Like at Home from 1 January 2026. Note also that the Commission item is from an MKD source file (the 2025 Enlargement Communication).

Different measures: the Real Estate Register "is digitalised" (exists as a digital register, NAP December 2025) against "lack of complete digitalisation" of registers such as immovable property (completeness of content and processes, May 2025). Both can be true.

Different measures and dates: SIGMA (2023) says all base registers are available in digital format; the 2025 programme says some essential registers are not completely digitalised. Digital availability and complete digitisation of records differ; SIGMA itself notes legacy problems with civil status records.

Unclear whether the same law: the Commission dates a law partially harmonising with the Open Data Directive "in line with the European Interoperability Framework" to July 2026, while Promo-LEX and the Government give Law 109/2025 (May 2025). It may be a later amending or interoperability law. If the Commission means Law 109/2025, its date is wrong and the link is confirmed. Check.
Same as LNK-001530: the July 2026 law in the Commission report may differ from Law 109/2025. Confirmed only if the Commission means Law 109/2025. Check.

Different measures: the Commission (report to September 2025) says "not yet aligned" with the Open Data Directive; the Government says Law 109/2025 only partially transposes it. Partial transposition is compatible with "not yet aligned".

Same law, two entry-into-force dates: the Commission says 10 December 2022; the Government says in force since 1 January 2025. Neither text mentions staged entry into force. If the law has deferred provisions, the link becomes apparent; check the final provisions of Law 124/2022.

Different reference points: the Government describes Law 124/2022 as originally adopted (partial transposition) and in the next sentence says it was updated by Law 117/2025; the Commission's "fully aligned with eIDAS 1.0" (2025 report) refers to the amended framework.
Different measures: 200,000 e-signature users (Commission, undated) against 246,674 valid qualified certificates (one user may hold several, across tokens, mobile ID and eID cards).

Different lists and dates: the MDED report (covering 2025, published April 2026) concerns inclusion of STISC as a provider in the EU trusted list after a conformity audit; the Commission (report to September 2026) says Moldova joined the EU third-country trusted list. Accession after April 2026 or a different listing explains the difference.
Different reference dates: the World Bank document (July 2024) was very likely drafted before the June 2024 launch the Commission reports.

Different scope: the factsheet (2024, before launch) says the EVOSign signing solution aligns with EU wallet standards and eIDAS; the 2025 programme says it must be extended to function as a full EU-standard wallet. Claimed standards alignment of a signing tool and missing wallet functions can both hold. The factsheet claim is promotional.

Different scope: SIGMA (2023) judges the interoperability infrastructure and register connections; the World Bank (2024) judges how well data systems are integrated in practice and the use of data. Both can be true.
Different measures and dates: over 2.6 million requests a day (AGE, 2024) against about 1.5 million successful queries a day (2025). Requests include failed ones.

Cannot both be true if the units are the same: SIGMA gives 665.7 million MConnect transactions in 2022 alone, while AGE gives 600 million data exchanges in total. The AGE page is also internally inconsistent (2.6 million a day would exceed 600 million within a year, noted at extraction). A unit difference (transaction against exchange) is possible but not stated. Treat the AGE total as unreliable.

Same matter and period: the Government (December 2025) says data exchange takes place "exclusively" through MConnect; the data protection authority (report on 2025) says state bodies continue to access personal data through COI technology, which lacks user identification. The government sentence may describe the legal requirement rather than practice. If read that way the link is apparent (law against practice), but it is worded as fact.

No conflict: the migration inspectorate refers to the government decision regulating the concept of the Fingerprint Register system and proposes amendments to it for EURODAC. It does not say an electronic biometric database with fingerprints and photos is operational or connected. The basis infers an existing system that the text does not state.

Different drafting dates: the December 2025 National Accession Programme draft (its context cites GD 687 of 15 October 2025) still proposes the roadmap, which the Commission says was approved in November 2025. The government text was most likely drafted before the approval.
